cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Pull a spring gently, let go, and watch it return.
Then it passes the center and comes back again.
Why doesn't it simply stop at the center?
The force restores it toward equilibrium, but its velocity carries it through.
That balance gives us oscillation.
Let's measure displacement from the equilibrium position, with right positive.
For simple harmonic motion, acceleration equals minus omega squared times
displacement.
The minus sign is the whole story of direction: right of center, acceleration
points left; left of center, it points right.
Its magnitude also grows in proportion to how far we move from center.
A repeating motion is not automatically simple harmonic.
It must satisfy this particular acceleration rule.
Period is the time for one complete cycle, returning to the same position and
direction of motion.
Frequency counts cycles per second.
Angular frequency counts radians of phase per second and equals two pi times
frequency.
If an oscillator makes two cycles per second, its period is half a second and
its angular frequency is four pi radians per second.
Now think for a moment.
At equilibrium, is acceleration largest?
No, it is zero.
Speed can still be largest there.
Never confuse zero acceleration with zero velocity.
That distinction is a favorite source of JEE mistakes.
Picture the horizontal shadow of a point moving around a circle at constant
angular speed.
The shadow moves between two ends.
This projection is a beautiful way to understand simple harmonic motion.
We write displacement as amplitude times the cosine of omega t plus initial
phase.
Amplitude sets the size of the motion; omega sets how quickly it repeats; phase
tells us where in that repeating cycle we are.
For zero initial phase, the particle begins at the positive end, not at the
center.
Differentiate displacement with respect to time: velocity is minus amplitude
times omega times sine of the same phase.
Differentiate again and acceleration becomes minus omega squared times
displacement, exactly our defining rule.
Let's use amplitude four centimeters and angular frequency five radians per
second.
At the positive end, displacement is zero point zero four meters.
Velocity is zero, while acceleration is minus one meter per second squared.
A quarter period later the particle crosses equilibrium moving in the negative
direction.
Its velocity there is minus zero point two meters per second and its
acceleration is zero.
Pause and imagine those two moments.
The turning point has no speed but a strong inward acceleration; the center has
the greatest speed but no acceleration.
For initial conditions, use both position and velocity to select phase.
Position alone usually leaves two possible phases, because a particle can visit
the same position while moving in opposite directions.
Now let's see where angular frequency comes from.
An ideal spring exerts a restoring force equal to minus spring constant times
displacement.
Newton's second law says mass times acceleration equals this force.
Divide by mass, compare with our simple harmonic motion rule, and omega squared
equals spring constant divided by mass.
So the period is two pi times the square root of mass divided by spring
constant.
This is not a formula to memorize blindly.
Greater mass means more inertia and a slower response.
A stiffer spring supplies more restoring force for the same displacement and
gives a faster response.
Take a half kilogram block on a spring of two hundred newtons per meter.
Omega is twenty radians per second.
The period is pi divided by ten seconds, about zero point three one four
seconds.
If the mass becomes four times larger with the same spring, what happens?
Give yourself a moment.
The square root becomes twice as large, so the period doubles, not quadruples.
Within the ideal Hooke law model, changing amplitude does not change period.
Real springs can leave this model at large extensions.
For a vertical spring, gravity stretches the spring to a new equilibrium.
Measure displacement from that new position.
The constant gravitational force cancels the equilibrium spring force, leaving
the same restoring rule for the additional displacement.
The period still depends on mass and spring constant, not on that equilibrium
extension by itself.
At the end of the motion the block stops for an instant.
Where has its kinetic energy gone?
Into the spring's potential energy.
At equilibrium the spring's potential energy, measured from the unstretched
position for our horizontal spring, is zero and kinetic energy is largest.
With no friction, the total stays constant: one half spring constant times
amplitude squared.
At displacement x, potential energy is one half spring constant times x
squared.
Subtract it from total energy and you get the kinetic energy.
That gives speed squared equal to omega squared times amplitude squared minus
displacement squared.
Notice that squaring loses the direction.
Use the actual part of the cycle to decide whether velocity is positive or negative.
Let's return to our half kilogram block and two hundred newtons per meter
spring, now with amplitude ten centimeters.
Total energy is one joule.
At displacement six centimeters, spring potential energy is zero point three
six joules, leaving zero point six four joules of kinetic energy.
The speed is one point six meters per second.
At the center it reaches two meters per second.
Here's a useful JEE check: at half the amplitude, potential energy is one
quarter of total energy, not one half.
Kinetic energy is the remaining three quarters.
Energy depends on displacement squared.
With damping the amplitude and mechanical energy decrease, so the constant
energy formula no longer describes the whole changing motion.
A swinging pendulum is another oscillator, but we must earn the simple harmonic
approximation.
Model the bob as a point mass on a light, inextensible string of length L.
Gravity has a tangential component opposite the angular displacement.
The exact tangential equation gives angular acceleration equal to minus g
divided by L times sine of theta.
That sine matters.
For a sufficiently small angle measured in radians, sine theta is approximately
theta.
The equation then becomes the simple harmonic rule, with omega squared equal to
g divided by L.
Its period is two pi times the square root of length divided by gravitational
acceleration.
Bob mass cancels out.
For a one meter pendulum and g equal to nine point eight meters per second
squared, the period is about two point zero one seconds.
If its length becomes four meters, the period becomes about four point zero one
seconds, twice the original value.
This assumes the same gravitational acceleration and small oscillations.
A large swing takes longer than this small angle formula predicts; don't claim
amplitude independence for every pendulum swing.
Let's summarize your problem solving routine.
Choose equilibrium, identify the restoring equation, check whether it is
proportional to displacement, and state the assumptions.
Then select a phase equation, period relation or energy equation depending on
the question.
Oscillations become much easier when you connect the equations to the actual
motion instead of treating each one as a separate trick.
